korea.title: Fiscal Consequences of AI Automation
korea.intro: This is a bottom-up accounting model of what AI automation does to Korea's public finances. To use this model, pick a scenario from the sidebar (each one is a published AI forecast) or set your own levers. Every number on this page is a change against a no-AI baseline, with NABO's projections coming first, and this adds to them. What the model shows is the tax base moving from wages and labor to profits, prices and compute, which are taxed at significantly lower rates. This disproportionately impacts the National Pension, Health Insurance, and Employment Insurance funds, which are funded exclusively by income and payroll tax.
korea.disclosure_note: All numbers are net of re-employment and demand effects, and include EI benefit outlays. AGI scenarios only cover cognitive work, meaning that they understate displacement in manual occupations, and every headline is quoted as a range.

captions.nps: The 2025 pension reform moved depletion from 2057 to 2065, buying eight years. The band shows how much of that automation takes back
captions.nhi: NABO projects depletion in 2029 under the medical reform plans. Automation shortens that depletion time.
captions.ei: The published plan rebuilds reserves to ₩21.8tn by 2029, relying on borrowing from the public funds. Erosion plus benefit outlays is what automation takes from that plan
captions.composition: The central scenario spreads damage almost evenly. The clerical epicentre is mid-wage, so every fund loses about 9% of its base by 2035, with the capped pension losing slightly most.
captions.contrast: A what-if scenario with 50% displacement concentrated in one group. High-wage automation mostly hits income tax, which goes to the general account, while low-wage automation hits the funds, with the pension hardest.
captions.workforce: Every worker out of the 12.4M modeled wage workers is in exactly one band each year. Displacement moves people down the stack, while re-employment and attrition move them out of limbo.
captions.wages: The wage index of workers who keep their jobs: raises funded from the survivor share push it up; labor-market slack pulls it down.
captions.budget: National revenue and the absolute deficit against the no-AI baseline, in ₩ trillions per year.
captions.ei_outlay: Benefit spending on the displaced, paid at the statutory rate. These outlays are what dominates the EI shortfall.
captions.tornado: Rank correlation with the chosen headline across the Monte Carlo draws. Red bars worsen the headline when raised
captions.map: Each province's occupation mix weighted by the BOK displacement-prone shares. This is descriptive only, and makes no provincial fiscal claims.

metrics.nps: Of the pension reform's 8 bought years, automation takes back

disclosures: Wage employees only, which is about 76% of Korean employment. The self-employed are treated qualitatively.
The establishment survey frame covers 12.4M of roughly 22M wage workers, over-represents larger firms, and excludes public administration.
Nine occupation groups by 24 wage brackets, which is deliberately coarse and transparently so.
Displacement is net. The model re-employs into a finite service floor, pays survivor raises, and propagates demand destruction.
Erosion counts revenue plus EI benefit outlays. NHI and NPS outlay responses and forgone investment income are not counted, and both omissions understate the damage.
Exposure is a reading of BOK's published chart, accepted because it reconciles with the printed aggregates. The ±0.5pp reading error is carried into the band.

nhi_share.label: NHI wage-linked revenue share
nhi_share.help: The share of Health Insurance revenue that scales with the wage base. The documented band is 0.65 to 0.97, with the midpoint as the default, pending the NHIS workplace split.

nps_share.label: NPS wage-linked revenue share
nps_share.help: The share of pension contributions that comes from workplace subscribers. The documented band is 0.75 to 0.95, with the midpoint as the default, pending the NPS yearbook split.

exposure_delta.label: Exposure reading (±0.5pp)
exposure_delta.help: The reading tolerance on BOK's published chart, carried as a scenario rather than averaged away.

demography_variant.label: Population scenario (KOSIS)
demography_variant.help: The published KOSIS 2022–2072 projections. Low, medium, and high scenarios only, with no interpolation between them.

reemployment_haircut.label: Re-employment wage cut (haircut)
reemployment_haircut.help: Re-employed workers earn (1 − haircut) × their old wage, floored at the statutory minimum wage. Evidence puts the typical haircut around 0.13, and 0.25 for long-tenure mass layoffs. A larger cut can bring households into 근로장려금 (EITC) range, which the model includes.

ui_weeks.label: Jobseeker benefit duration (weeks)
ui_weeks.help: The 구직급여 window. During it, displaced workers draw the statutory benefit, which is tax-exempt, and contribution payments stop entirely.

lfp_exit_rate.label: Labor force exit rate (of exhausted)
lfp_exit_rate.help: The share of exhausted workers who leave the labor force each year. This is the dominant adjustment path in the China-shock evidence.

income_tax_mult.label: Income tax multiplier
income_tax_mult.help: A multiplier on the baseline personal income tax take, national and local. It also scales the income-tax base movements from displacement, raises, and re-employment. Contributions are unaffected.

corp_tax_mult.label: Capital taxes multiplier
corp_tax_mult.help: A multiplier on the baseline corporate tax take of ₩84.6tn (2025 receipts). The compute pool and robot tax levers are unaffected.

cons_tax_mult.label: Consumption taxes multiplier
cons_tax_mult.help: A multiplier on the baseline VAT take of ₩79.2tn (2025 receipts).

interest_rate.label: Interest rate on national debt
interest_rate.help: New deficits compound into debt at this rate.

vat_pp.label: VAT increase (statutory +pp)
vat_pp.help: Statutory VAT points added to the 10% rate, applied to the ₩792tn effective base measured from 2025 receipts (NABO Focus 137). The base erodes as displacement rises, and the scoring is static.

nps_mandate_share.label: NPS automation dividend (share of AI profits)
nps_mandate_share.help: A mandated NPS equity share of after-tax automation profits, which flows to the fund and never through the treasury.

corp_to_funds.label: Automation corporate recapture to the funds
corp_to_funds.help: The share of automation-driven corporate tax revenue (the corporate offset plus the compute-pool tax) transferred from the general account to the three funds, allocated in proportion to each fund's erosion. The deficit worsens by exactly the transfer.

rail.agi_disclosure: This scenario only covers cognitive work, since there is no published Korean robot-exposure data, so it understates displacement in manual occupations.
rail.api_down: Custom settings need the compute service, which is not reachable; showing the closest preset instead. Preset browsing works fully offline.

overlays.heading: Policy responses

kr-vat.label: +1pp VAT (10% → 11%)
kr-vat.help: One statutory point on the effective base of ₩792tn, measured from 2025 receipts. The base erodes as displacement rises.

kr-nps-mandate.label: NPS automation dividend (20% of AI profits)
kr-nps-mandate.help: A mandated NPS equity share of after-tax automation profits, which flows to the fund and never through the treasury.

overlays.vat_readout: Static scoring, with no behavioral response.

about:
This is a bottom-up accounting model of what AI automation does to US public finances. Note that all models are wrong, but some are useful; ideally this model is useful to some.

**How it works.** The model prices every displaced worker's taxes and benefits at the occupation-by-state level (33,369 cells against BLS, BEA, Census, and other data), then follows the wages firms stop paying to where they end up going: profit, lower prices, raises for the remaining staff, and compute costs. Then each destination is taxed at its real rate. However, wages are taxed at roughly 25-30%, while their replacements are taxed far less. All 51 states must balance their budgets every year, and the lost paychecks and state austerity cause demand destruction, leading to further layoffs. 

**What it isn't.** This is not a forecast, but rather is a scenario calculator and simulator. The presets are based on published forecasts (Acemoglu, Korinek, AI 2027, AI 2040, etc), whose projections are translated into lever positions. Every result is a change against a no-AI baseline, with the deficits the CBO already projects coming first.

**Deliberate simplifications of this model.** There are two significant structural decisions that this model makes. First, capital income does not spend, with retained profit only impacting the economy through corporate taxes; there is no shareholder-consumption or investment channel, with the latter likely being a significant source of economic growth. Second, there is no task creation: displaced workers re-enter only through a fixed re-employment rate into a finite set of low-exposure occupations; automation never endogenously creates new kinds of work. These simplifications are deliberate. The history of automation shows that offsets will eventually arrive, but this model asks what the fiscal impacts will be if the offsets arrive late or never. Fiscal authorities will still need to be able to respond to this scenario, but consider the numbers to be in a world with no offsets.

**Why trust the model.** The code is open source and machine-checked: around 350 automated tests, including eight accounting identities re-verified in every period of every run, so workers and dollars cannot multiply or vanish. With every lever switched off the system reproduces the static calculation bit-exact, and the results triangulate against three independent external models (Acemoglu, Windfall Trust, RAND). Claude Fable 5 and Opus 4.8 wrote the code in this project under those checks and constraints.

**Acknowledgements.** Sincere appreciation to Princeton's Summer Social Impact Internship Fund for funding my internship at Constellation Institute. Further thanks to Jeff Alstott for mentoring and guiding me on this project.

[Source code](https://github.com/AlexWszolek/AI-Automation-Fiscal-Simulator) · [Technical report](https://aifiscalimpacts.alexwszolek.com/report.html) · [Preset evidence](https://aifiscalimpacts.alexwszolek.com/evidence.html)"

Federal revenue and the absolute deficit. Revenue falls faster than employment because high-paying occupations are more exposed to automation, and with the tax schedule being progressive the budget loses its best taxpayers first.

The destinations of the wages firms stop paying. Every dollar goes to one destination, and each is taxed at a different rate: profit around 18%, prices around 2%, raises at full labor rates, and compute at the capital rate.
Jobs lost because displaced households stop spending and states cut budgets. This tracks income withdrawal, so stimulus (UBI, raises) re-employs these workers.
What the raises cost firms vs the extra federal tax they generate, which is the mechanism that rebuilds the labor tax base.
The state shortfall, annual and cumulative, before any response, so the deficit states would run if they could borrow. This is what the first years could look like while legislatures catch up.

The consequence of the response you chose above: revenue recovered by rate hikes vs spending cuts (including cuts FORCED where the cap binds). Try 'Raise taxes' vs 'Cut spending' — the federal picture changes too, because both withdraw demand differently.

To use this model, pick a scenario from the sidebar (each one is a published AI forecast) or set your own levers. Every number on this page is a change against a no-AI baseline, meaning that the deficits the CBO already projects come first, and this adds to them. learn_more:
#### The data

The model is based on data from the BLS, BEA, Census, and other sources, measuring the US economy in 2024. Importantly, every file carries control totals that must always stay the same for every model run: 163.2 million workers, \$15.0 trillion in total compensation, \$29.3 trillion GDP, \$4,983 billion in federal receipts, and others. If this fails, then the model will stop. The model runs on a set of 33,369 occupation-by-state cells, each of which contains wages, automation exposure scores, household archetypes, and state tax rules. These cells cover 154.0 million workers, or 94%, with the rest in suppressed or unmatched cells that are excluded from the model.

| Source | Data contribution |
|---|---|
| BLS OEWS 2024 | employment and wages for 833 occupations, 71 industries, all 51 jurisdictions |
| BEA 2024 NIPA | capital income, corporate profits, and government receipts by stream |
| Yale Budget Lab AI exposure | how cognitively automatable each occupation is |
| Webb robot exposure | how physically automatable each occupation is, from robot patents |
| ACS PUMS 2024 | who workers live with, so filing status, household income, children |
| PolicyEngine-US | means-tested benefit entitlements by state, family shape, and income |
| 2025 tax schedules | the brackets and FICA parameters behind the tax engine |
| CBO Projections | the revenue and expenses of the federal government, serving as a baseline |

#### How a displaced worker is priced

For each of roughly 33,000 occupation-by-state cells, the model answers one question: if this worker loses this wage, what happens to tax revenue at every level of government? There are five channel that the model takes into account.

- **Income tax**: based on the change in wages, income tax brackets are properly re-evaluated at houshold income. This does not use average rates, elasticites, or anything else: this is how this worker's taxes would actually change.
- **Payroll (FICA)**: uses the exact schedule, taking into account the Social Security cap, which is the wage range where one could potentially expect AI automation to start first.
- **Transfers**: new benefit claims are based on an offline version of PolicyEngine data. There are two stages, first during unemployment insurance, and after it runs out. Medicaid and SNAP step-ups mostly arrive at UI exhaustion, not immediately at the layoff.
- **Corporate recapture**: the wage that a firm stops paying becomes taxable profit, which the model taxes at the highest plausible rate, based on industry averages. 
- **Consumption**: losses in state consumption taxes due to a drop in spending

Importantly, the model integrates over the full wage distribution inside each cell rather than only using average workers. As safety-net programs are "humps" and "cliffs", with EITC rising then falling, SNAP phasing out, and Medicaid eligibility being a cliff, using average wages would understate transfer costs. In some cells that straddled a threshold, transfer costs were understated by a factor of eight. 


#### The dynamic model

The simulation then runs the economy, so all of the cells, forward one year at a time, based on the following steps:

1. An adoption ceiling sets how much feasible work is automated that year; this is cumulative. Physical automation occurs later than cognitive automation, based on user/preset settings.
2. Firms use the saved wage bill in one of four ways: compute spending, retained profit, price cuts for consumers, and raises for surviving workers. All lost wages must go to one of these four destinations.
3. Survivor wages are funded from the saved wage bill, never out of thin air. They are taxed through the previously described tax bracket schedules.
4. The macro block applies the price cuts and productivity increases to real output. Importantly, deflation is not fed into nominal tax math.
5. The federal government books the net loss and borrows to cover the deficit. 
6. All 51 states must balance their budgets every year. This is done by rate hikes and/or spending cuts.
7. Lost take-home pay, along with state austerity, leads to demand destruction, leading to induced layoffs the following year. This loop is made so that it converges and does not spiral, which would be unrealistic; this is checked at every instance.


#### Trustworthiness

- Eight accounting identities are re-verified on every period of every run, to ensure conservation. Every worker is in exactly one of seven states that sum baseline employment, every dollar goes to exactly one place, every state gap closes to zero, and five more. If a new fiscal flow were to not be conserved, this would break the model.
- If all levers are switched off, then the full system reproduces the static calculation, and is bit-exact.
- There around around 350  tests that cover identities, channel numbers, and behavioral pins from displacement literature. 
- Every result is a delta against a no-AI baseline. This is not a forecast of the whole economy, just what automation changes. The sensitivity tornando shows which levers are most impactful, for transparency.


#### What the model leaves out

Naturally, this model has simplifications, some of which are listed below:
- Saved compensation by firms is fully converted to taxable surplus, which in reality would lead to a larger fiscal gap
- The Fed does not respond to either deflating prices or significant unemployment, not following its dual mandate; the model overstates the fiscal gap in crisis scenarios
- Within-job augmentation is not represented, which one can expect to lead to more productive and profitable firms, which could result in higher income and corporate taxes, overstating the gap
- Compute/robot taxes do not affect firm behaviors and prices, which would slow down adoption
- Robot exposure is anchored to the current patent stock, which understates potential robotics adoption rates


#### Validation

There are three important independent external models that triangulate the results. First is Windfall Trust's fiscal simulator. This model reproduces their sign and ordering everywhere (worse with more displacement, worse with less value capture, etc), but at roughly half their magnitudes. This is reasonable, as they used an average-OECD tax base vs the actual US system. Second is RAND's 10-point unemploument shock, which lands in their order of magnitude once their deflation mechanisms (which was temporarily turned on for this test) is applied. Finally, the Acemoglu preset's GDP gain is within his ~1.1 percent bound. None of the presets were tuned to hit these numbers.

adopt0.help: Where the cumulative adoption ceiling starts. Early payroll evidence (Brynjolfsson's 'Canaries') puts the realized start near 0.02.
adopt0.label: Automated by year 1 — % of feasible work

adopt1.help: A cumulative diffusion ceiling: the automated stock reaches feasibility × this share by the horizon, so 0.6 means 60% of the feasibly-automatable jobs are automated by the end.
adopt1.label: Automated by the final year — % of feasible work

atax.help: A federal levy on the automated jobs' saved compensation, paid from retained profit and corporate-deductible. It ships at 0, as the literature-anchored rates live in the policy overlays: Costinot-Werning is roughly 0.3-1%, not 7%.
atax.label: Automation (robot) tax — share of the automated comp bill

attrition.help: Attrition due to retirement, mortality, and discouragement. Fiscally neutral, as the baseline counterfactual retires as well. Natural attirtion prevents exhausted workers from existing in the workforce indefinitely.
attrition.label: Natural attrition of long-term unemployed / yr

auto_cost.help: The fraction of saved wages that firms spend on compute/automation costs to replace workers. The evidence points to 0.3-0.5 in build-out years and ~0.05-0.10 in steady state.
auto_cost.label: Cost of automation (fraction of saved comp → compute)

ceiling.help: The cap on the still-employed wage index. Raises beyond it spill to profit or prices (spillover below); raises themselves are funded from the routed survivor share and re-taxed at full marginal rates.
ceiling.label: Raise ceiling (× baseline wage)

cog.help: Of the work cognitively exposed to AI (the Yale exposure index), the share that is technically automatable. Literature anchors run from ~0.15 (bare LLMs, Eloundou) to ~0.55 (LLMs plus the software they can build); 1.0 is AGI.
cog.label: Cognitive feasibility (AI capability)

compute_rate.help: The effective tax on the compute-capital pool. ~0.05 is the post-TCJA rate on equipment and software capital; 0.27 is parity with domestic capital (the compute-parity overlay).
compute_rate.label: Compute pool — effective tax rate

cons_mult.help: A multiplier on the $874B state sales-and-excise and $102B federal excise baselines, plus scaling of the state consumption-tax channel. Note that these bases are quite small compared to income taxes.
cons_mult.label: Consumption taxes multiplier

corp_mult.help: A multiplier on the $492B federal and $172B state baseline corporate receipts, plus scaling of the capital-recapture bundle. This does not affect compute-pool and robot tax levers.
corp_mult.label: Capital taxes multiplier

demand.help: An Okun-style multiplier, where laid-off workers lead to demand destruction and thus induced layoffs.
demand.label: Second-round demand multiplier

elasticity.help: How survivors' market wages respond to labor-market slack. Negative means that AI substitues for labor and thus depresses wages, while positive is augmentation and pulls up wages.
elasticity.label: Market wage response to slack (− substitute / + complement)

growth.help: This is roughly 2% real plus 2% inflation. This grows the GDP denominator so that debt-to-GDP is more accurate.
growth.label: Baseline trend growth (nominal, %-GDP denominators)

haircut.help: The re-employed earn (1 − haircut) × their old wage, floored at a state service wage. The evidence implies a typical haircut of around 0.13, and 0.25 for high-tenure mass layoffs. A bigger cut can drop the household into EITC/SNAP/Medicaid eligibility, which is taken into account.
haircut.label: Re-employment wage cut (haircut)

income_mult.help: A multiplier on the $2,403B federal and $536B state baseline individual-income receipts, plus scaling on the income tax base shifts, so displaced losses, the raises' recapture, the tax on UI, and reabsorbed-worker income. Payroll (FICA) is not affected.
income_mult.label: Income tax multiplier

interest.help: New deficits accumulate into debt at this rate. ~0.04 matches the discount-rate anchor used in the AGI presets. There is literature on interest rates increasing substantially due to AI putting substantial upward pressure on growth rates, but this model does not account for that.
interest.label: Interest rate on federal debt

lfp.help: The share of benefit-exhausted workers who leave the labor force each year onto disability insurance, which is an $18k/yr outlay. This is the dominant adjustment margin in the China-shock evidence.
lfp.label: LFP exit / SSDI rate (of exhausted)

n_periods.help: Simulation length. Presets are based on their respective timelines.
n_periods.label: Horizon (years)

phys.help: The same idea for physical work (Webb's robot-patent exposure). Anchored to current robot technology, as dexterity and care work score near zero even at 1.0.
phys.label: Robotics feasibility (physical work)

price.help: The share competed away into lower consumer prices. This is great for consumers, but this is only taxed through state consumption taxes, which makes it a substantial leak in tax revenue.
price.label: Saved wages to lower prices pass-through

price_pt.help: The share of the firms' price cuts that actually deflates the price level. By design it moves only the real and %-of-GDP views, as nominal tax dollars are never deflated.
price_pt.label: Price pass-through to price level

prod_pt.help: The output-weighted real-GDP gain, so automating the entire workforce raises GDP by this fraction. Acemoglu's "The Simple Macroeconomics of AI" implies ~0.15; the micro and AGI evidence implies 0.5-1.0. It cushions the %-of-GDP views.
prod_pt.label: Productivity impact on GDP

rate_cap.help: The political and economic ceiling on rate increases, as a multiple of the current rates. Once a state hits it, the remainder becomes forced spending cuts.
rate_cap.label: Max feasible rate hike

reab.help: The annual rate at which long-term displaced workers find new, lower-wage work. The evidence shows 0.6-0.75 in normal labor markets (Farber) and 0.05-0.10 in the China-shock adjustment; 0 makes displacement permanent. The refuge is finite, with this rate scaling down as automation reaches the low-exposure service work the re-employed move into, and stops entirely once it is gone.
reab.label: Reabsorption rate per year

reab_baumol.help: How strongly re-employment wages ride the economy's productivity gains: the work humans still do gets expensive as everything else gets cheap (Baumol's cost disease, but in this case benefiting labor). At 1.0, a +20% productivity economy pays re-employed workers +20%. This is how wages can rise despite mass displacement.
reab_baumol.label: Re-employed wage — Baumol pull

reab_crowd.help: How strongly displaced workers flooding into service work bid its wage down, with the wage falling with the previous year's labor-market slack. Evidence from the China-shock supports a meaningful value, which competes directly with Baumol pull.
reab_crowd.label: Re-employed wage — crowding pressure

retained.help: The share of saved wages, net of automation costs, that firms keep as profit. This is taxed at effective corporate rates of around 17%, which is significantly below the labor-tax it replaces.
retained.label: Saved wages to retained profit pass-through

rob_base.help: How the build-out is shaped, with 1.0 being a linear build-out. The idea behind an industrial explosion scenario is that robots build factories that build robots, so the ramp starts slow and finishes fast. At 1.5, half of all capacity is built in the final fifth of the lag.
rob_base.label: Robot build-out growth (exponential base)

robotics_lag.help: Physical automation requires AI-driven industrial capacity first. This adjusts how long it takes to the robot channel to ramp up, with 0 meaning that the capacity exists from day one.
robotics_lag.label: Robotics capacity build-out lag (years)

spillover.help: Where raises above the ceiling go instead. 1.0 sends all of it to retained profit, which is corporate-taxed, while 0.0 sends it all to lower prices.
spillover.label: Un-absorbable raise pass-through to profit/price

state_cut.help: How states close their revenue gap, which they can either do by raising rates on the remaining wage base or by cutting spending.
state_cut.label: Share of the gap closed by spending cuts

state_resp.help: The closure rule for every state, every year: 'raise taxes' raises rates on the remaining wage base up to the cap, 'cut spending' takes the whole gap out of budgets, and 'mix' splits it by the slider.
state_resp.label: What do states do?

ubi.help: A universal payment per baseline worker, booked as a federal outlay.
ubi.label: UBI per worker per year

ubi_recapture.help: The share of the UBI outlay the government gets back. This includes an income-tax clawback plus the means-tested benefits the UBI displaces; the clawback is around 25% in practice.
ubi_recapture.label: UBI recapture

ui_weeks.help: The unemployment-insurance window. During it, displaced workers draw benefits (45% replacement, capped) and are taxed on them; most means-tested benefits step up at exhaustion, not at displacement.
ui_weeks.label: UI duration (weeks)

unbounded.help: Removes the raise ceiling entirely, so survivors absorb whatever the routed share funds.
unbounded.label: Unbounded raise (optimistic)

metrics.help: Workers who are not employed in the final year that counterfactually would be. This includes workers on unemployment insurance, exhausted, exited to SSDI, or laud off by the demand shortfall. This metric excludes the re-employed and retirements.
metrics.label: Jobs lost (final yr)

metrics.help: The decline in workers still employed at their original wage, against the modeled baseline. The re-employed at lower wages count as not employed here.
metrics.label: Employment

metrics.help: The total federal income-tax revenue lost to displacement, summed over the horizon. This is the largest fiscal channel.
metrics.label: Federal income tax lost (cumulative)

metrics.help: The absolute federal deficit at the final year, which includes the CBO baseline plus the shock's net effect. The line below restates it as a share of productivity-and-trend-adjusted GDP.
metrics.label: Federal deficit (final yr)

metrics.help: Summation of all deficits, accumulated with interest. This is relative to the CBO baseline. Negative values means that the automation impacts pay debt down, as capital recoveries outgrow the losses.
metrics.label: Federal debt (Δ cumulative)

metrics.help: The signed change in the federal balance in the final year, where negative is worse. It reconciles to the fiscal summary table below.
metrics.label: Net fiscal impact (final yr)

metrics.help: State fiscal shortfall, what they must close before any rate hikes and cuts. The state section below expands on this.
metrics.label: State shortfall (final yr)

metrics.help: Compares real output against the baseline, so it takes into account the productivity dividend. In extreme scenarios this is large and positive while the fiscal picture collapses, as the abundance arrives as profit and lower prices, but nor as taxed wages.
metrics.label: Real GDP effect

prose.detail_caption: This is the source data that every chart and number uses. Columns ending in _B are billions of dollars; _M, millions of workers.
prose.map_caption: This map shows the final-year loss as a share of each state's own tax revenue, which measures how hard automation impacts that state's budget. Hovering over a state shows the dollar values of its net position, the shortfall, how the chosen response closes it, and the implied rate hike on its remaining workers.
prose.share_caption: Anyone who opens the link will see the current configuration. The browser's address bar stays in sync as well, so copying that also works.
prose.states_intro: Unlike the federal government, states cannot borrow to offset a revenue shock. Nearly all operate under balanced-budget rules, so a shortfall has to be met within the year. A state's response to this is primarily political, which is why this is a controlable level: states can either raise taxes on the people still working, cut spending, or a mix of the two. However, there are some caveats. First, legislatures lag, and rainy-day funds and deferrals may mean that the first years or two will look like the shortfall chart rather than the closre. Second, whichever response they choose takes demand out of the same economy that is shedding jobs, which leads to futher demand destruction. Third, it is a possibility that the federal government takes up some of the burden, which could potentially complicate responses.
prose.summary_signs: Revenue lines are signed revenue changes, with negative meaning lost revenue; outlay lines are spending changes, with positive meaning more spending; net fiscal impact is the negative of the deficit change, with negative being worse. Flows sum into Total, and levels show the final year.
prose.table_caption: A state "hits its cap" when the rate increase it needs exceeds the feasibility ceiling, and the remainder becomes forced spending cuts. Negative net positions are states whose survior-wage gains outweight their losses.
prose.units_cbo_help: The CBO view divides each year by that same year's projected total federal revenue (February 2026 baseline), answering how big the shock is against the money the government actually expects to have.
prose.view_help: The two summary views group the same reconciled flows differently; 'Detailed per-year' is every raw model column.
